opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the assignment itself isn't very fancy. It's a small, open-ended reinforcement-learning problem. You get an environment, maybe a rough baseline, and twenty-four hours. There isn't one correct answer, and that's on purpose. I'm not really testing whether you know the latest algorithm. I'm watching how you behave when nobody is holding your hand.

The first thing I look at is whether the person actually gets something working end to end. Many people spend twenty hours designing a beautiful method and then run out of time with nothing that trains. Reliable people get a dumb baseline running in the first hour or two. Then they iterate. That habit says a lot about how they'll work on a real team, where a working thing beats a perfect plan.

The second thing is honesty about results. RL is very noisy. You can run one seed, get a nice curve, and convince yourself you've made progress. When someone writes "I tried three seeds, the variance is huge, I'm not sure this improvement is real," that's a very strong positive signal for me. When someone shows one pretty curve and claims victory, I get nervous, even if the number is higher. In research, the most expensive thing isn't a failed experiment. It's a wrong conclusion that everyone builds on for months.

Third, I look at what they did when things broke, because something always breaks. Did they debug systematically? Did they check whether the reward was what they thought, look at actual rollouts, and sanity-check the environment? Or did they just keep turning hyperparameters? You can tell from the write-up whether someone actually looked at the data.

Finally, the write-up itself. Can they explain in a page what they tried, what worked, what didn't, and what they'd do with another week? That's basically the daily job. If you can communicate clearly under time pressure, I can trust you with a direction and not have to check on you every day.

So for me, "reliable" doesn't mean "got the highest score." It means that if I give you a fuzzy problem, you'll come back with something real, tell me the truth about it, and I can believe what you say. Twenty-four hours turns out to be enough to see that pretty clearly.

r001.rationale: The response evaluates practical execution, honest reporting, debugging, and communication; it does not compare AI use with unaided coding ability.

r002.rationale: It describes assessing the written report, but does not say a follow-up discussion reveals AI delegation or lack of understanding.

r003.rationale: It does not mention sleep or treat sacrificing sleep as evidence of valuing the opportunity.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll draft the guest response now.

The assignment itself is actually very simple. I give the candidate a small reinforcement learning task, something like getting an agent to learn in a toy environment, and I say you have 24 hours, send me whatever you have. The task is deliberately not hard. If you know RL you can get a working baseline in two or three hours. What I'm looking at is not whether they solve it. It's everything around the solving.

The first thing I look at is what they do when something doesn't work. Because something always doesn't work. The reward curve flattens, or there's some instability in training, or a hyperparameter is clearly wrong. The unreliable person either hides it, or they just write "it didn't converge" and stop. The reliable person tells me exactly what they tried, what they observed, and what their current hypothesis is, even if they didn't fix it. That's really the whole signal. Can I trust what this person reports back to me when I'm not watching?

The second thing is whether they can separate what they know from what they guess. A lot of people with strong backgrounds will write a very confident-sounding writeup where half the claims aren't actually backed by their own experiments. I'd much rather see someone say, I think this is because of X, but I only ran one seed so I'm not sure. In research that kind of honesty compounds. If I can't tell which of your results are solid, then all of your results become useless to me.

Then there's the practical stuff. Did they check in code that I can actually run? Did they spend the 24 hours wisely, or did they spend 20 hours building infrastructure and 4 hours on the actual problem? Did they read the task carefully, because I'll often put in a small detail that changes the problem, and some people just skip it and solve the problem they assumed I asked.

And honestly, the last thing is just effort and taste. 24 hours is a constraint. Some people do the minimum. Some people do the minimum and then add one extra experiment that shows me they were genuinely curious about the question. That second group is who I want to work with. Because the day-to-day of research is not solving clean problems. It's being alone with a messy problem for a long time, and I need to know that when you come back, what you tell me is true.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability, experiments, and honest reporting, but does not compare AI use with unaided coding ability.

r002.rationale: It does not describe a post-assignment discussion or identify candidates who delegated work to AI without understanding it.

r003.rationale: It mentions effort and curiosity under the 24-hour constraint, but does not discuss sacrificing sleep as a signal of how much the opportunity matters.

astra-6.text:
I’m looking less at whether they get an impressive result in 24 hours and more at how they approach an open-ended problem. Can they turn it into something concrete, get a baseline running, and choose a useful experiment? With reinforcement learning, you can spend the whole day running something and still learn very little. So I want to understand why they made each decision and what the results actually tell them.

The follow-up discussion is especially important. What did you finish? What didn’t work? Which conclusions are supported by the experiments, and which are still guesses? A negative result can be perfectly good if they’ve investigated it carefully and can explain the limitations. Reliability means I can trust their account of the work, including the unfinished parts, and see that they know what to do next.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m less interested in whether they get a spectacular result in 24 hours than in how they handle an open-ended problem. Can they turn it into something manageable, establish a baseline, and check whether their implementation is actually doing what they think it is doing?

Reinforcement learning is useful here because a curve going up doesn’t necessarily mean your idea worked, and a curve staying flat doesn’t immediately tell you what went wrong. You have to investigate. I want to understand what they tried, why they tried it, and what evidence led them to the next step.

The write-up matters, too. Can they clearly distinguish what they demonstrated from what they suspect? If something failed, can they explain the failure honestly? Someone who produces a modest result with a clear, reproducible account can give me more confidence than someone who shows an impressive number but can’t explain where it came from. Reliability is about whether I can trust their conclusions and build on their work.
